claim: Notch signalling components remain expressed in neural crest after induction.
source: Our analysis reveals that Notch components remain expressed in NC after induction, suggesting that Notch signalling may also be involved in later aspects of NC development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing expression of Notch components (notch1a, dlb, dld, her4) in migrating neural crest cells, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Notch signalling levels vary widely between premigratory trunk neural crest cells.
source: Moreover, analysis of the Notch activity reporter line 12xNRE:egpf (Moro et al., 2013) shows that Notch signalling levels vary widely between premigratory TNC (Figure 1), suggesting that Notch may play a role after TNC induction.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from the Notch reporter line 12xNRE:egfp showing variable GFP expression levels in premigratory TNC cells, as shown in Figure 1.

claim: Notch inhibition impairs trunk neural crest induction up to 11 hours post-fertilization.
source: Our results showed that Notch inhibition impairs TNC induction up to 11 hours post-fertilization (hpf; Figure 2) and confirmed previous reports that induction of the cranial and vagal NC populations is independent of Notch signalling (Cornell and Eisen, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing reduced or absent crestin expression in DAPT-treated embryos at different developmental stages, as shown in Figure 2D, and cites previous work by Cornell and Eisen, 2000.

claim: Induction of cranial and vagal neural crest populations is independent of Notch signalling.
source: Our results showed that Notch inhibition impairs TNC induction up to 11 hours post-fertilization (hpf; Figure 2) and confirmed previous reports that induction of the cranial and vagal NC populations is independent of Notch signalling (Cornell and Eisen, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous work by Cornell and Eisen, 2000, and confirmed by the authors' experimental results.

claim: Notch inhibition at 12 hpf reduces all trunk neural crest derivatives including neurons, glia, and pigment cells.
source: We found a reduction in all TNC derivatives (neurons, glia, and pigment cells; Figure 3A–F) upon Notch inhibition, suggesting that Notch activity is important in a process subsequent to induction, yet prior to differentiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data for glial marker mbp, neuronal marker bdh, and pigmentation analysis showing reduced expression/presence upon DAPT treatment, as shown in Figure 3A-F.

claim: Notch inhibition reduces the number of trunk neural crest cell chains formed and their ventral advance.
source: Analysis of crestin expression showed a reduction in the number of TNC cell chains formed and in their ventral advance upon DAPT treatment (Figure 3G–J), which likely explains the lack of TNC derivatives at later stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing reduced crestin expression and chain formation upon DAPT treatment, as shown in Figure 3G-J.

claim: Notch signalling blockade delays trunk neural crest migration rather than completely halting it.
source: To this end, embryos were treated with DAPT from 12 hpf for 6–12 hr and processed for crestin expression. Decreased numbers of migratory chains were observed at all timepoints, but as embryos developed new chains were formed, indicating that the blockade of Notch signalling delays TNC migration (Figure 3K).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course analysis showing that new chains form over time despite DAPT treatment, as shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Genetic inhibition of Notch using dominant-negative Suppressor of Hairless produces similar migration defects as chemical inhibition.
source: Comparable results were obtained by inhibiting Notch genetically in embryos where the dominant-negative form of Suppressor of Hairless is under the control of a heat shock element (Latimer et al., 2005; hs:dnSu(H); Figure 3L).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of migratory chain formation in hs:dnSu(H) embryos showing similar reduction as DAPT treatment, as shown in Figure 3L, and cites the genetic tool from Latimer et al., 2005.

claim: Notch gain of function and loss of function result in almost identical phenotypes with similar reduction of trunk neural crest chain numbers.
source: To our surprise, Notch gain of function (GOF) and loss of function (LOF) resulted in almost identical phenotypes, both showing a similar reduction of TNC chain numbers (Figure 3L).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data showing similar reduction in chain numbers for both Notch GOF (hs:Gal4;UAS:NICD) and LOF (hs:dnSu(H)) conditions, as shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Precise regulation of Notch signalling levels is required for trunk neural crest migration.
source: Taken together, these results show that precise regulation of Notch signalling levels is required for TNC migration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both Notch GOF and LOF produce similar migration defects, suggesting that intermediate levels are required.

claim: Under Notch inhibition, trunk neural crest leader cells are unable to retain the front position and are overtaken by followers.
source: Under Notch inhibition (treatment with γ-secretase inhibitor Compound E; Richter et al., 2017), TNC remain motile with a single cell initiating the movement of the chain, but in contrast to control treatment (DMSO) the leader cell is unable to retain the front position and is overtaken by one or several followers (Figure 4A and C, Figure 5A and B, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data showing leader overtaking events in Compound E-treated embryos, as shown in Figure 4C and quantified in Figure 5B, and cites Richter et al., 2017 for the inhibitor.

claim: Notch inhibition leads to reduced ventral advance of trunk neural crest with most leader cells unable to move beyond the neural tube/notochord boundary.
source: This loss of group coherence corresponds with a reduction in ventral advance, with most leader cells unable to move beyond the neural tube/notochord boundary (NT/not; Figure 4C, Figure 5A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data and quantification showing reduced ventral distance traveled by cells under Notch inhibition, as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Under Notch inhibition, trunk neural crest leader cells have decreased speed and directionality.
source: Analysis of single-cell tracking showed that under Notch inhibition leader cells also have decreased speed and directionality (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cell tracking data showing reduced speed and directionality in Notch-inhibited conditions, as shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Somite development and neuron formation are not affected by Notch inhibition at the axial level where trunk neural crest migration was analyzed.
source: However, this appears unlikely as somite development (formation, patterning, and differentiation) and neuron formation are not affected by Notch inhibition at the axial level analysed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization and antibody staining data showing normal expression of somite markers (cb1045, myod, F59) and neuronal markers (dld, Znp1, acetylated tubulin) upon DAPT treatment, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Autonomous inhibition of Notch signalling in neural crest phenocopies chemical inhibition with leader cells unable to retain front position and reduced ventral advance.
source: We found that autonomous inhibition of Notch signalling in NC phenocopies the chemical inhibition. Leader cells are unable to retain the front position, being overtaken by followers, and ventral advance is reduced with cells accumulating at the NT/not boundary (Figure 4D, Figure 5A–C, Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data from Sox10:Kalt4;UAS:dnSu(H) embryos treated with tamoxifen showing similar phenotypes to chemical inhibition, as shown in Figure 4D and Figure 5A-C.

claim: Notch activity is autonomously required in trunk neural crest for identity allocation.
source: Moreover, leader cells adopt followers' migratory parameters, showing decreased speed and directionality (Figure 5D and E), confirming that Notch activity is autonomously required in TNC for identity allocation, and suggest that in the absence of Notch signalling a homogenous group of followers is established.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cell-autonomous Notch inhibition experiments showing that leader cells adopt follower characteristics, as shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: In the absence of Notch signalling, a homogenous group of followers is established.
source: Moreover, leader cells adopt followers' migratory parameters, showing decreased speed and directionality (Figure 5D and E), confirming that Notch activity is autonomously required in TNC for identity allocation, and suggest that in the absence of Notch signalling a homogenous group of followers is established.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that all cells adopt follower characteristics under Notch inhibition.

claim: Notch overactivation leads to loss of group coherence, leader overtaking by followers, and impaired ventral advance.
source: Similar results were obtained in both experimental conditions: group coherence is lost, leader cells are overtaken by followers, and ventral advance is impaired (Figure 4F, Figure 5A–C, Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data from Notch GOF conditions (Sox10:Kalt4;UAS:NICD) showing these phenotypes, as shown in Figure 4F and Figure 5A-C.

claim: In Notch gain of function conditions, follower cells adopt leader characteristics, moving with increased speed but following less directional trajectories.
source: Interestingly, in Notch GOF conditions follower cells adopt leaders' characteristics, moving with increased speed, but all cells in the chain follow less directional trajectories, which hinders the ventral advance of the group (Figure 5D and E), indicating that all cells in the chain migrate as leaders.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cell tracking data showing increased speed but reduced directionality in Notch GOF conditions, as shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: In control conditions, phox2bb transcripts are highly enriched in leader cells from early stages of migration.
source: In control conditions, phox2bb transcripts are highly enriched in the leader cells from early stages of migration (Figure 6A, B, and G; Alhashem et al., 2022a).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope data showing phox2bb expression predominantly in leader cells, as shown in Figure 6A, B, and G, and cites Alhashem et al., 2022a.

claim: Upon Notch overactivation, phox2bb is expressed by all cells in the chain.
source: Consistent with expectations, upon Notch overactivation phox2bb is expressed by all the cells in the chain (Figure 6C, D, and G), while its expression is absent when Notch is inhibited (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope data showing phox2bb expression in all cells under Notch GOF conditions, as shown in Figure 6C, D, and G.

claim: phox2bb expression is absent when Notch is inhibited.
source: Consistent with expectations, upon Notch overactivation phox2bb is expressed by all the cells in the chain (Figure 6C, D, and G), while its expression is absent when Notch is inhibited (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAscope data showing absence of phox2bb expression under Notch inhibition, as shown in Figure 6E-G.

claim: Notch activity controls phox2bb expression and allocates trunk neural crest migratory identity.
source: These data show that Notch activity controls phox2bb expression and allocates TNC migratory identity.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined data showing that phox2bb expression correlates with Notch activity levels and migratory identity.

claim: Trunk neural crest with high levels of Notch signalling express phox2bb and become leaders, while cells with low Notch activity migrate as followers.
source: In summary, our in vivo and molecular data show that Notch signalling is required autonomously in TNC for migratory identity allocation. TNC with high levels of Notch express phox2bb and become leaders, while cells with low Notch activity migrate as followers.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined data from Notch manipulation experiments and phox2bb expression analysis.

claim: Alterations of Notch signalling lead to a homogeneous trunk neural crest group with a single migratory identity that is unable to undergo collective migration.
source: Alterations of Notch signalling lead to a homogeneous TNC group with a single migratory identity that is unable to undergo collective migration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both Notch GOF and LOF produce homogeneous populations (all leaders or all followers) that cannot migrate collectively.

claim: Notch lateral inhibition is the mechanism responsible for trunk neural crest migratory identity acquisition.
source: Taken together, these data suggest Notch lateral inhibition as the mechanism responsible for TNC migratory identity acquisition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pattern of Notch activity and the outcomes of Notch manipulation experiments.

claim: Simulations with homogeneous cells cannot match all in vivo trunk neural crest migration scores, confirming that cell heterogeneity is required.
source: We first simulated chains composed of homogeneous cells and systematically covaried all parameters. We found no parameter combination able to match all scores, confirming our previous findings that cell heterogeneity is required for TNC migration (Figure 7C; Richardson et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results showing that homogeneous cell simulations cannot recapitulate in vivo behavior, as shown in Figure 7C, and cites Richardson et al., 2016.

claim: The computational model is only able to recapitulate control conditions when the difference between leaders and followers is maximal for all variables.
source: Interestingly, the model is only able to recapitulate control conditions when the difference between leaders and follower is maximal for all variables. Nevertheless, it is unable to recapitulate Notch GOF and LOF phenotypes (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results showing that maximal parameter differences are required to match control conditions, as shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Several parameter combinations from 1:2 and 1:3 leader/follower ratios can recapitulate in vivo control conditions as well as Notch gain and loss of function phenotypes.
source: Interestingly, we found that several parameter combinations from the 1:2 and 1:3 leader/follower ratios were able to recapitulate in vivo control condition, as well as the loss of group coherence and ventral advance observed in Notch GOF (all leader simulation) and LOF (all follower simulation; Figure 4B, E, and G, Figure 5, Figure 4—video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results showing that 1:2 and 1:3 ratios can match both control and Notch-altered conditions, as shown in Figure 4B, E, G and Figure 5.

claim: In the computational model, CIL intensity is the parameter that most differs between leader and follower cells.
source: Next, we used this method to assess the importance of each of the model parameters. CIL intensity appears to be the parameter that most differ between leader and follower cells, while heterogeneity in the other parameters is not essential (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear discriminant analysis of the computational model showing CIL intensity as the most important distinguishing parameter, as shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The computational model predicts that trunk neural crest chains are formed of leaders and followers in a 1:2 or 1:3 ratio.
source: Finally, the model anticipates that TNC chains are formed of leaders and followers in a 1:2 or 1:3 ratio.
evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling results showing that these ratios best recapitulate in vivo behavior.

claim: Leader cells are almost twice as big as follower cells during migration.
source: Cell size is a prominent characteristic distinguishing leader from follower cells. Leaders are almost twice as big as followers during migration and this difference is evident before migration initiation (Richardson et al., 2016), suggesting that size disparity arises at birth or shortly thereafter.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation of Richardson et al., 2016 showing size differences between leaders and followers.

claim: The size difference between leader and follower cells is evident before migration initiation.
source: Cell size is a prominent characteristic distinguishing leader from follower cells. Leaders are almost twice as big as followers during migration and this difference is evident before migration initiation (Richardson et al., 2016), suggesting that size disparity arises at birth or shortly thereafter.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation of Richardson et al., 2016 and suggests that size differences arise early.

claim: The asymmetric division of a single progenitor cell gives rise to a larger cell that becomes a leader and a smaller sibling that migrates as follower.
source: Tracking analysis shows that the asymmetric division of a single progenitor cell in each body segment gives rise to a larger cell that becomes a leader (102 ± 20 µm2), and a smaller sibling that migrates as follower (72 ± 9 µm2; Figure 8A and B, Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging and tracking data showing asymmetric division producing cells of different sizes that adopt different identities, as shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: All other progenitors divide symmetrically, giving rise to two follower cells.
source: In contrast, all other progenitors divide symmetrically, giving rise to two follower cells (87 ± 27 µm2; Figure 8C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging and tracking data showing symmetric divisions producing cells of similar size that both become followers, as shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: Leader progenitor divisions are spatially restricted to the anterior quarter of the premigratory area in each segment.
source: We also noticed that the leader progenitors' divisions are spatially restricted to the anterior quarter of the premigratory area in each segment, while the followers' progenitor divisions take place across the premigratory area (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial analysis of division positions showing leader progenitors divide in a restricted anterior region, as shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Follower progenitor divisions take place across the premigratory area.
source: We also noticed that the leader progenitors' divisions are spatially restricted to the anterior quarter of the premigratory area in each segment, while the followers' progenitor divisions take place across the premigratory area (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial analysis of division positions showing follower progenitors divide throughout the premigratory area, as shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Most leader cells divide during migration (86% follow M→D pattern).
source: Interestingly, we found that the patterns of cell division correlate with cell identity. Most leader cells divide during migration (M→D: 86%), while the bulk of follower cells divide before migration initiation (D→M: 90%, Figure 8H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of division patterns showing that 86% of leader cells follow the M→D pattern, as shown in Figure 8H.

claim: The bulk of follower cells divide before migration initiation (90% follow D→M pattern).
source: Interestingly, we found that the patterns of cell division correlate with cell identity. Most leader cells divide during migration (M→D: 86%), while the bulk of follower cells divide before migration initiation (D→M: 90%, Figure 8H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of division patterns showing that 90% of follower cells follow the D→M pattern, as shown in Figure 8H.

claim: 74% of leader cells divide at the neural tube/notochord boundary (65.3 ± 9.6 µm).
source: These patterns result in leader and follower cells dividing at distinct positions, 74% of leaders divide at the NT/not boundary (65.3 ± 9.6 µm), while 85% of followers divide mostly within the premigratory area or in the dorsal-most region of the somite (42 ± 12.4 µm; Figure 8I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of division positions showing that 74% of leaders divide at the NT/not boundary, as shown in Figure 8I.

claim: 85% of follower cells divide mostly within the premigratory area or in the dorsal-most region of the somite (42 ± 12.4 µm).
source: These patterns result in leader and follower cells dividing at distinct positions, 74% of leaders divide at the NT/not boundary (65.3 ± 9.6 µm), while 85% of followers divide mostly within the premigratory area or in the dorsal-most region of the somite (42 ± 12.4 µm; Figure 8I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of division positions showing that 85% of followers divide in the premigratory area or dorsal somite, as shown in Figure 8I.

claim: Leader and follower cells progress asynchronously through the cell cycle.
source: Together, these results show that leader cells arise from the asymmetric division of a progenitor. Thereafter, leader and follower cells show distinct locations and patterns of division, suggesting that leaders and followers progress asynchronously through the cell cycle, which may influence their migratory behaviour.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that leaders and followers have different division patterns and locations.

claim: The S-phase inhibitor aphidicolin blocks over 94.7% ± 4.5% of mitotic figures after 3 hours of treatment.
source: The S-phase inhibitor aphidicolin blocks over 94.7% ± 4.5% of mitotic figures after 3 hr of treatment, while the G2/M inhibitor genistein prevents 90% ± 10% of divisions within 6 hr, but neither treatment affects NC induction (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of mitotic figures showing that aphidicolin blocks over 94.7% of divisions, as shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The G2/M inhibitor genistein prevents 90% ± 10% of divisions within 6 hours.
source: The S-phase inhibitor aphidicolin blocks over 94.7% ± 4.5% of mitotic figures after 3 hr of treatment, while the G2/M inhibitor genistein prevents 90% ± 10% of divisions within 6 hr, but neither treatment affects NC induction (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of mitotic figures showing that genistein prevents 90% of divisions, as shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither aphidicolin nor genistein treatment affects neural crest induction.
source: The S-phase inhibitor aphidicolin blocks over 94.7% ± 4.5% of mitotic figures after 3 hr of treatment, while the G2/M inhibitor genistein prevents 90% ± 10% of divisions within 6 hr, but neither treatment affects NC induction (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing normal crestin expression at 16 hpf after aphidicolin treatment, as shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Inhibition of cell cycle progression results in reduced numbers of migratory chains and decreased ventral advance.
source: Inhibition of cell cycle progression by either of the treatments resulted in reduced numbers of migratory chains and decreased ventral advance (control 19 ± 2, genistein 10 ± 3, aphidicolin 6 ± 2 chains; Figure 9A–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data and quantification showing reduced chain numbers and ventral advance upon cell cycle inhibition, as shown in Figure 9A-H.

claim: Premigratory trunk neural crest cells actively extend protrusions and move along the anteroposterior axis but are unable to migrate ventrally when cell cycle is inhibited.
source: This result was not due to the loss of cell motility as premigratory TNC cells actively extend protrusions and move along the anteroposterior axis but are unable to migrate ventrally (Figure 9—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data showing that cells remain motile but cannot migrate ventrally under cell cycle inhibition, as shown in Figure 9—video 1.

claim: Trunk neural crest cells reinitiate migration and form new chains upon cell cycle inhibitor withdrawal.
source: Importantly, these effects were not a consequence of cell death or the permanent impairment of motility as TNC reinitiate migration and form new chains upon drug withdrawal (Figure 9G and H), showing that active cell cycle progression is required for migration.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification showing recovery of chain formation after drug withdrawal, as shown in Figure 9G and H.

claim: Active cell cycle progression is required for trunk neural crest migration.
source: Importantly, these effects were not a consequence of cell death or the permanent impairment of motility as TNC reinitiate migration and form new chains upon drug withdrawal (Figure 9G and H), showing that active cell cycle progression is required for migration.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observation that cell cycle inhibition blocks migration but cells can recover upon drug withdrawal.

claim: Most leader cells initiate migration in S-phase (79%).
source: Tracking analysis shows differential cell cycle progression, with most leader cells initiating migration in S-phase (79%), while followers start movement during G1 (77%; Figure 9I and J, Figure 9—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of Sox10:FUCCI embryos showing that 79% of leaders initiate migration in S-phase, as shown in Figure 9I and J.

claim: Follower cells start movement during G1 (77%).
source: Tracking analysis shows differential cell cycle progression, with most leader cells initiating migration in S-phase (79%), while followers start movement during G1 (77%; Figure 9I and J, Figure 9—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of Sox10:FUCCI embryos showing that 77% of followers initiate migration in G1, as shown in Figure 9I and J.

claim: Cell cycle progression is required for migration and leader and follower cells initiate movement at different points of the cell cycle.
source: These results show that cell cycle progression is required for migration and that leader and follower cells initiate movement at different points of the cell cycle, suggesting an intimate connection between cell growth and movement.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined data from cell cycle inhibition experiments and FUCCI analysis.

claim: There is no significant difference in the total length of the cell cycle between leaders and followers (13.6 ± 1.2 and 13.3 ± 1.4 hours, respectively).
source: Measurements of the time span between two consecutive mitoses showed no significant differences in the total length of the cell cycle between leaders and followers (13.6 ± 1.2 and 13.3 ± 1.4 hr, respectively; Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cell cycle length showing no significant difference between leaders and followers, as shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Leader cells have a short G1 phase (3.2 ± 0.6 hours) but remain for twice as long in S-phase (8.7 ± 1.3 hours).
source: We found striking differences in the time spent in G1- and S-phase between leader and follower cells. Leaders present a short G1 (3.2 ± 0.6 hr) but remain for twice as long in S-phase (8.7 ± 1.3 hr).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cell cycle phase lengths using PCNA-GFP showing that leaders have short G1 and long S-phase, as shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Follower cells remain for twice as long in G1 (7.4 ± 2.7 hours) than in S-phase (4.6 ± 2.8 hours).
source: Followers, on the other hand, present the opposite distribution, remaining for twice as long in G1 (7.4 ± 2.7 hr) than in S-phase (4.6 ± 2.8 hr; Figure 10C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cell cycle phase lengths using PCNA-GFP showing that followers have long G1 and short S-phase, as shown in Figure 10C and D.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the length of G2 (leaders 1.6 ± 0.4 hours; followers 1.5 ± 0.3 hours) or M (leaders 0.6 ± 0.1 hours; followers 0.5 ± 0.1 hours) between leaders and followers.
source: No significant differences were observed in the length of G2 (leaders 1.6 ± 0.4 hr; followers 1.5 ± 0.3 hr) or M (leaders 0.6 ± 0.1 hr; followers 0.5 ± 0.1 hr).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cell cycle phase lengths showing no significant difference in G2 or M phase between leaders and followers.

claim: Leader and follower cells present marked differences in the length of G1- and S-phase, suggesting that cell cycle progression may regulate their migratory behaviour.
source: These data show that leader and follower cells present marked differences in the length of G1- and S-phase, suggesting that cell cycle progression may regulate their migratory behaviour.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that leaders and followers have different G1 and S-phase lengths.

claim: Neither the total cell cycle length nor the number of trunk neural crest cells were affected by alterations of Notch signalling.
source: To investigate this question, we measured the total length of the cell cycle and the length of each phase under control and Notch-inhibited conditions. Neither the total cell cycle length (Figure 11A) nor the number of TNC (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) were affected by alterations of Notch signalling.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification showing no significant difference in total cell cycle length or cell number under Notch inhibition, as shown in Figure 11A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Upon Notch inhibition, leader cells lose their characteristic cell cycle progression pattern and behave as followers, with a long G1 and a short S-phase.
source: Remarkably, we found significant differences in the length of G1- and S-phase upon Notch inhibition. Leader cells lose their characteristic cell cycle progression pattern and behave as followers, with a long G1 and a short S-phase (Figure 11B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cell cycle phase lengths showing that leaders adopt follower-like G1 and S-phase lengths under Notch inhibition, as shown in Figure 11B.

claim: Notch inhibition abolishes the size difference between migratory leader and follower cells, with all cells presenting the average follower's area.
source: Furthermore, Notch inhibition abolishes the size difference between migratory leader and follower cells, with all cells presenting the average follower's area (Figure 11C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cell area showing no significant difference between leaders and followers under Notch inhibition, as shown in Figure 11C and D.

claim: Notch activity defines trunk neural crest migratory identity by regulating cell cycle progression.
source: These data show that Notch activity defines TNC migratory identity by regulating cell cycle progression, cells with low Notch activity remain for longer in G1 behaving as followers.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined data showing that Notch inhibition changes cell cycle progression and migratory identity.

claim: Cells with low Notch activity remain for longer in G1 behaving as followers.
source: These data show that Notch activity defines TNC migratory identity by regulating cell cycle progression, cells with low Notch activity remain for longer in G1 behaving as followers.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observation that Notch inhibition leads to longer G1 phase and follower behavior.

claim: Notch inhibition reduces the dispersion of the follower population's cell cycle phase lengths, with standard deviations cut almost by half.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that Notch inhibition also changes the cell cycle behaviour of the followers' population. While the followers' average length of cell cycle phases is not altered, the dispersion of this population is significantly reduced, with standard deviations cut almost by half (from 2.7 hr to 1.42 hr for G1 and from 2.8 hr to 1.38 hr for S; Figure 11B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification showing reduced standard deviation in follower cell cycle phase lengths under Notch inhibition, as shown in Figure 11B.

claim: In control conditions, leader cells show a normal distribution with a single peak for G1- and S-phase.
source: In control conditions, leader cells show a normal distribution with a single peak for G1- and S-phase, as expected for a homogeneous population.
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency distribution analysis showing a single peak for leaders, as shown in Figure 11E and F.

claim: In control conditions, follower cells present a bimodal distribution, with the smaller peak coinciding with that of leader cells and accounting for 26% of followers in G1 and 31% in S-phase.
source: Followers, on the other hand, present a bimodal distribution, with the smaller peak coinciding with that of leader cells, and accounting for 26% of followers in G1- and 31% in S-phase (Figure 11E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency distribution analysis showing a bimodal distribution for followers with a subset resembling leaders, as shown in Figure 11E and F.

claim: The bimodal distribution of follower cells fulfills the predictions of the computational model that best recapitulates trunk neural crest migration when chains are composed of leaders and followers in a 1:2 or 1:3 ratio.
source: Strikingly, these results fulfil the predictions of our in silico model that best recapitulates TNC migration when chains are composed of leaders and followers in a 1:2 or 1:3 ratio.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that approximately 25-30% of followers have leader-like cell cycle characteristics, consistent with a 1:3 or 1:2 leader:follower ratio.

claim: Upon Notch inhibition, the bimodal distribution of the follower population is lost, with all cells grouped at the major mean.
source: Furthermore, upon Notch inhibition the bimodal distribution of the follower population is lost, with all cells grouped at the major mean (Figure 11G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency distribution analysis showing loss of bimodal distribution under Notch inhibition, as shown in Figure 11G and H.

claim: Closer analysis of normal phox2bb expression shows increased expression in followers at position 3 in addition to that in leaders.
source: Consistent with these data, closer analysis (at higher magnification) of normal phox2bb expression shows increased expression in followers at position 3 in addition to that in leaders (Figure 11I–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by high-magnification RNAscope images showing phox2bb expression in the third follower cell, as shown in Figure 11I-N.

claim: The levels of Notch activity in trunk neural crest allocate migratory identity by controlling cell cycle progression.
source: Taken all together, our data demonstrate that the levels of Notch activity in TNC allocate migratory identity by controlling cell cycle progression and that migratory chains are formed of one leader cell for every three followers.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined data from Notch manipulation, cell cycle analysis, and phox2bb expression experiments.

claim: Migratory chains are formed of one leader cell for every three followers.
source: Taken all together, our data demonstrate that the levels of Notch activity in TNC allocate migratory identity by controlling cell cycle progression and that migratory chains are formed of one leader cell for every three followers.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined data from computational modeling, cell cycle distribution analysis, and phox2bb expression patterns.

claim: Progression through G1/S is required for trunk neural crest delamination in chicken embryos.
source: This is consistent with studies in chicken embryos, showing that progression through G1/S is required for TNC delamination, and that NC continue cycling as they migrate (Burstyn-Cohen and Kalcheim, 2002; Théveneau et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous work by Burstyn-Cohen and Kalcheim, 2002 and Théveneau et al., 2007.

claim: Neural crest cells continue cycling as they migrate in chicken embryos.
source: This is consistent with studies in chicken embryos, showing that progression through G1/S is required for TNC delamination, and that NC continue cycling as they migrate (Burstyn-Cohen and Kalcheim, 2002; Théveneau et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous work by Burstyn-Cohen and Kalcheim, 2002 and Théveneau et al., 2007.

claim: The timing of G1/S transition depends on cell size and the dilution of the nuclear retinoblastoma protein.
source: It is possible that these differences arise from the fact that leaders are larger than followers. It has been shown that the timing of G1/S transition depends on cell size and the dilution of the nuclear retinoblastoma protein (Zatulovskiy and Skotheim, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation of Zatulovskiy and Skotheim, 2020.

claim: Cyclins B and D phosphorylate cytoskeleton regulators, resulting in increased cell migration and tumour invasion.
source: Cyclins B and D have been shown to phosphorylate cytoskeleton regulators, resulting in increased cell migration and tumour invasion (Blethrow et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2020; Chi et al., 2008; Hirota et al., 2000; Li et al., 2006; Manes et al., 2003; Song et al., 2008; Zhong et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations showing that cyclins can regulate cytoskeleton and migration.

claim: Rac1 activity oscillates during the cell cycle being highest at S-phase when cells are most invasive.
source: Furthermore, Rac1 activity, which is required for migration, oscillates during the cell cycle being highest at S-phase when cells are most invasive (Kagawa et al., 2013; Walmod et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations of Kagawa et al., 2013 and Walmod et al., 2004.

claim: Cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors interact with RhoA and ROCK, enhancing motility.
source: CDKIs, on the other hand, interact with RhoA- and ROCK-enhancing motility (Bendris et al., 2015; Creff and Besson, 2020; Yoon et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations of Bendris et al., 2015, Creff and Besson, 2020, and Yoon et al., 2012.

claim: Enhanced motility increases actin branching, which in turn can accelerate the G1/S transition.
source: Interestingly, enhanced motility increases actin branching, which in turn can accelerate the G1/S transition (Molinie et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation of Molinie et al., 2019.

claim: Notch can regulate cell cycle through the transcriptional induction of cyclins A and D, and the inhibition of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors.
source: Depending on the cell type, Notch can regulate cell cycle through the transcriptional induction of cyclins A and D, and the inhibition of CDKIs (Campa et al., 2008; Dabral et al., 2016; Ridgway et al., 2006; Rizzo et al., 2008; Rowan et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations showing Notch regulation of cell cycle components.

claim: Notch activity is enhanced at the G1/S transition.
source: Conversely, cell cycle progression can impact on Notch signalling. Notch activity is enhanced at the G1/S transition, while cells become refractory to Notch during G2/M (Ambros, 1999; Carrieri et al., 2019; Hunter et al., 2016; Nusser-Stein et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations of Ambros, 1999, Carrieri et al., 2019, Hunter et al., 2016, and Nusser-Stein et al., 2012.

claim: Cells become refractory to Notch during G2/M.
source: Conversely, cell cycle progression can impact on Notch signalling. Notch activity is enhanced at the G1/S transition, while cells become refractory to Notch during G2/M (Ambros, 1999; Carrieri et al., 2019; Hunter et al., 2016; Nusser-Stein et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations of Ambros, 1999, Carrieri et al., 2019, Hunter et al., 2016, and Nusser-Stein et al., 2012.

claim: Studies in cancer cell lines have shown that activation or inhibition of Notch signalling hinders migration.
source: For example, studies in cancer cell lines have shown that activation or inhibition of Notch signalling hinders migration, similar to what we observe in TNC (Konen et al., 2017), while the maintenance of collective migration depends on the regulation of cell proliferation during angiogenesis (Costa et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation of Konen et al., 2017.

claim: The maintenance of collective migration depends on the regulation of cell proliferation during angiogenesis.
source: For example, studies in cancer cell lines have shown that activation or inhibition of Notch signalling hinders migration, similar to what we observe in TNC (Konen et al., 2017), while the maintenance of collective migration depends on the regulation of cell proliferation during angiogenesis (Costa et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation of Costa et al., 2016.
